title: Part II: Analysis of Financial Statements

topics.title: Analysis of financial statements: meaning, significance and objectives

learn.hook: A balance sheet is a photo; analysis is the X-ray. It shows what the numbers really mean for profit and safety.
points: Analysis of financial statements is the systematic study of relationships among items in the financial statements to judge profitability and financial position.
Analysis breaks data into meaningful groups and relationships; interpretation explains what those results mean. Analysis comes first, interpretation follows.

Users: finance manager (planning), top management (efficiency), trade payables (short-term solvency), lenders (long-term solvency and interest-paying ability), investors (profitability and growth), labour unions (capacity to pay wages), and government/analysts.
Objectives: assess earning capacity, managerial efficiency, short-term and long-term solvency, make inter-firm and intra-firm comparisons, and help forecasting and budgeting.

example.q: A supplier wants to sell goods on 60 days' credit to a company. What will the supplier mainly look for in its financial statements?
steps: A trade payable cares about getting paid soon.
That depends on the company's short-term solvency (liquidity).
example.answer: Short-term solvency – its ability to pay current liabilities.

learn.reallife: Credit-rating agencies such as CRISIL and ICRA analyse company statements before rating bonds that Indian investors buy.

games.title: Analysis basics
items: Interpretation comes before analysis.
Analysis organises the data; interpretation explains it afterwards.
Comparing a firm's results with another firm's is inter-firm comparison.
Intra-firm compares the same firm across periods or divisions.
Analysis helps in forecasting and budgeting.
Past trends guide future plans.
Only shareholders use financial analysis.
Lenders, creditors, managers, unions and government also use it.

quiz.q: Analysis of financial statements means:
options: studying relationships among items in financial statements to judge profitability and financial position
quiz.explain: It works on finished statements to draw meaning.
steps: Analysis is the systematic study of relationships among items in financial statements.
Its aim is to judge profitability and financial position.
Answer: studying relationships among items in financial statements to judge profitability and financial position

quiz.q: Analysis differs from interpretation because:
options: analysis arranges and relates data; interpretation explains the meaning of the results
analysis is only for tax purposes
quiz.explain: Interpretation builds on analysis.
steps: Analysis arranges and relates the data.
Interpretation then explains what the results mean.
Answer: analysis arranges and relates data; interpretation explains the meaning of the results

quiz.q: Which user is most interested in long-term solvency?
quiz.explain: Long-term lenders want assurance of interest and principal over years.
steps: Debenture-holders and long-term lenders want interest and principal over years.
So they care most about long-term solvency.
Answer: Debenture-holders and long-term lenders

quiz.q: Which user is most interested in short-term solvency?
quiz.explain: Suppliers want to be paid within the credit period.
steps: Suppliers want payment within the credit period.
So trade payables care most about short-term solvency.
Answer: Trade payables (suppliers)

quiz.q: Comparing this year's performance of Company X with its own previous years is:
quiz.explain: Intra = within the same firm.
steps: Comparing a firm with its own past years is within the same firm.
That is intra-firm comparison.
Answer: intra-firm comparison

quiz.q: Labour unions use financial analysis mainly to judge:
options: the company's capacity to pay wages and bonus
quiz.explain: Profitability and liquidity show the room for wage demands.
steps: Unions want to know how much the company can pay.
They judge its capacity to pay wages and bonus.
Answer: the company's capacity to pay wages and bonus

quiz.q: Which is an objective of financial analysis?
options: Assessing the earning capacity of the business
quiz.explain: Objectives include judging earning capacity, efficiency and solvency.
steps: Objectives include assessing earning capacity, efficiency and solvency.
Journal entries and cash books are recording, not analysis.
Answer: Assessing the earning capacity of the business

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Analysis of financial statements helps in forecasting.
Reason (R): Trends found from past data give a basis for estimating future performance.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Past trends help predict future figures.
steps: A: analysis helps forecasting – true.
R: past trends give a basis for estimating the future – true.
That is why analysis helps forecasting.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks analysis is only about the past

teach.ask: Gappu asks why anyone would analyse financial statements. Explain its meaning, users and objectives.
teach.praise: Excellent! Analysis studies relationships to judge profitability and solvency – useful to investors, lenders and managers.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what does a supplier look for when analysing a company?

revise.summary: Analysis of financial statements studies relationships among their items to judge profitability and financial position; interpretation explains the results. Different users seek different information, and objectives include judging earning capacity, efficiency, solvency and comparisons.
remember: Intra-firm: same firm over years; inter-firm: different firms
traps: Interpretation comes after analysis, not before
Suppliers care about short-term, not long-term, solvency
Comparing a firm with itself is intra-firm, not inter-firm

learn.hook: A doctor has a stethoscope, BP cuff and blood test. An analyst has four tools too – and like all tools, they have limits.
points: Tools: comparative statements, common-size statements, ratio analysis and cash flow analysis (trend analysis is also used).
Horizontal analysis compares figures across two or more periods (e.g. comparative statements); it is also called dynamic analysis.
Vertical analysis studies relationships among items of one period (e.g. common-size statements); it is also called static analysis.

Limitations: ignores price-level changes, ignores qualitative aspects, is based on historical data, can be affected by window dressing, is influenced by differing accounting policies, and may suffer from personal bias.

example.q: An analyst expresses every item of this year's Statement of Profit and Loss as a percentage of revenue from operations. Which tool and type of analysis is this?
steps: Expressing items as % of a common base is a common-size statement.
It uses one period only, so it is vertical analysis.

learn.reallife: Equity research teams in Mumbai combine all four tools – comparing years, common-sizing, ratios and cash flows – before recommending a stock.

games.title: Tools and limits
items: Common-size statements are a tool of vertical analysis.
They relate items within one period.
Comparative statements are a tool of vertical analysis.
They compare periods – horizontal analysis.
Different accounting policies can make inter-firm comparison misleading.
A limitation of analysis.
Financial analysis fully captures the quality of management.
Qualitative aspects are ignored.
Ratio analysis is a tool of financial analysis.
It is one of the main tools.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a tool of analysis of financial statements?
quiz.explain: A trial balance checks arithmetical accuracy of ledger balances; it is not an analysis tool.
steps: Tools: comparative statements, common-size statements, ratio analysis, cash flow analysis.
A trial balance only checks arithmetical accuracy, so it is NOT a tool.
Answer: Trial balance
quiz.mistake: Treats every accounting statement as an analysis tool

quiz.q: Horizontal analysis compares:
options: figures of two or more periods
quiz.explain: It looks across time.
steps: Horizontal analysis looks across time.
It compares figures of two or more periods.
Answer: figures of two or more periods

quiz.q: Vertical analysis is also called:
quiz.explain: It relates items of a single period.
steps: Vertical analysis relates items of one period.
It is also called static analysis.
Answer: static analysis

quiz.q: A common-size balance sheet is an example of:
quiz.explain: It expresses items of one period as % of total assets.
steps: A common-size balance sheet expresses one period's items as % of total assets.
That is vertical analysis.
Answer: vertical analysis

quiz.q: A comparative statement of profit and loss for 2024-25 and 2025-26 is an example of:
quiz.explain: It compares two periods.
steps: A comparative statement compares two periods side by side.
That is horizontal analysis.
Answer: horizontal analysis

quiz.q: Two firms use different depreciation methods, so their profits are not comparable. This limitation is:
quiz.explain: Policy differences distort comparisons.
steps: Different depreciation methods make profits not comparable.
That limitation is differences in accounting policies.
Answer: differences in accounting policies

quiz.q: Which is a limitation of financial analysis?
options: It ignores qualitative factors such as management quality
quiz.explain: Non-monetary factors are left out.
steps: Forecasting, solvency and comparison are uses.
Ignoring qualitative factors like management quality is a limitation.
Answer: It ignores qualitative factors such as management quality

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Financial analysis may give misleading results in times of high inflation.
Reason (R): Financial statements ignore price-level changes.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Historical-cost figures do not reflect inflation, so analysis can mislead.
steps: A: analysis may mislead in high inflation – true.
R: statements ignore price-level changes – true.
That is why analysis can mislead.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why inflation matters

teach.ask: Gappu wants to analyse a company. Tell him the tools and the limits.
teach.praise: Spot on! Comparative, common-size, ratios and cash flow – with horizontal and vertical views, and known limits.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: is a common-size statement horizontal or vertical analysis?

revise.summary: The tools of analysis are comparative statements, common-size statements, ratio analysis and cash flow analysis. Horizontal (dynamic) analysis compares periods; vertical (static) analysis relates items of one period. Analysis has limitations like ignoring inflation and qualitative factors.
remember: Limitations: price-level changes, qualitative aspects, historical data, window dressing, policy differences, bias
traps: A trial balance is not a tool of analysis
Common-size statements are vertical, not horizontal, analysis
Comparative statements are horizontal, not vertical, analysis

learn.hook: Revenue grew from ₹10 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh. Good – but did expenses grow faster? Comparative statements answer in two columns: absolute change and % change.
points: A comparative statement shows figures for two (or more) years side by side, with absolute change and percentage change.
Absolute change = Current year − Previous year. Percentage change = Absolute change ÷ Previous year × 100.
Comparative balance sheet compares items of equity, liabilities and assets; comparative statement of profit and loss compares revenue, expenses and profit.
Interpretation: e.g. if revenue grows faster than expenses, profit margins improve; if current liabilities rise faster than current assets, liquidity weakens.

example.q: Revenue from operations: 2024-25 ₹10,00,000; 2025-26 ₹12,50,000. Expenses: ₹6,00,000 and ₹7,20,000. Prepare the comparative figures.
steps: Expenses: change = ₹1,20,000; % = 20%.

learn.reallife: Business newspapers in India report a company's quarterly revenue and profit 'YoY growth' – that's a comparative statement in a headline.

items.text: Comparative statements are a tool of ___ analysis.

quiz.q: Revenue ₹10,00,000 in 2024-25 and ₹12,50,000 in 2025-26. Percentage change:
steps: Answer: 25%

quiz.q: Expenses ₹6,00,000 → ₹7,20,000. Absolute change:
steps: Absolute change = current − previous.

quiz.q: PBT ₹4,00,000 → ₹5,30,000. Percentage change:
steps: Answer: 32.5%

quiz.q: Trade receivables fell from ₹2,00,000 to ₹1,80,000. Percentage change:
steps: Answer: -10%

quiz.q: Revenue rose 25% and expenses rose 20%. This suggests that:
quiz.explain: When revenue grows faster than expenses, profit grows faster than revenue.
steps: Revenue grew 25%, expenses only 20%.
Revenue growing faster than expenses means profit grows faster.
So the profit margin has improved.
Answer: profit margin has improved
quiz.mistake: Thinks rising expenses always mean lower profit

quiz.q: Current assets rose 5% while current liabilities rose 30%. The likely interpretation:
quiz.explain: Liabilities growing much faster than assets reduce liquidity.
steps: Current liabilities grew 30%, current assets only 5%.
Liabilities growing much faster weakens short-term liquidity.
Answer: short-term liquidity has weakened
quiz.mistake: Ignores the faster growth of liabilities

quiz.q: Total assets ₹20,00,000 → ₹25,00,000. Percentage change:
steps: Answer: 25%

quiz.q: In a comparative balance sheet, the base for computing % change of each item is:
options: total assets of the current year
the previous year's figure of that item
quiz.explain: Comparative % change uses the earlier year as base; common-size uses totals.
steps: In a comparative statement, % change uses the previous year's figure of the same item as base.
Answer: the previous year's figure of that item

teach.ask: Gappu has two years of figures. Explain how to prepare and read a comparative statement.
teach.praise: Spot on! Absolute change, then % change on the previous year, and read what the trends say.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: do we divide by the previous year or the current year?

revise.summary: A comparative statement shows two or more years side by side with absolute change (current − previous) and percentage change (change ÷ previous × 100), and is used to judge trends in profitability and liquidity.
remember: Absolute change = current year − previous year
Base = previous year's figure of the same item
traps: Divide by the previous year, not the current year
A fall gives a negative % change
Don't use totals as the base in comparative statements; that is common-size

learn.hook: Compare a ₹100-crore company with a ₹10-lakh one? Turn both into percentages and suddenly they speak the same language.
points: Common-size statement of profit and loss: each item as a % of revenue from operations (revenue = 100).
Common-size balance sheet: each item as a % of total assets (or total equity and liabilities) (total = 100).
They show the structure (composition) of the statements and allow comparison between firms of different sizes and across years.
They are a tool of vertical analysis.

example.q: Revenue from operations ₹10,00,000; cost of materials consumed ₹6,00,000; employee benefits ₹1,00,000; other expenses ₹1,00,000. Prepare common-size percentages.
steps: Revenue = 100%.
Employee benefits = 10%; other expenses = 10%.

learn.reallife: Comparing Zomato and a small local food-delivery start-up is easier when you see marketing cost as a % of revenue for both.

games.title: Common-size checks
items: In a common-size statement of P&L, revenue from operations is taken as 100.
All items are % of revenue.
In a common-size balance sheet, each item is a % of total assets.
Total assets = 100.
Common-size statements compare two years using the previous year as base.
That is a comparative statement.
Common-size statements help compare firms of different sizes.
Percentages remove the size effect.
Common-size statements are a tool of horizontal analysis.
They are vertical analysis.

quiz.q: In a common-size statement of profit and loss, each item is expressed as a percentage of:
quiz.explain: Revenue from operations is the base (100).
steps: In a common-size statement of profit and loss, revenue from operations is the base (100).
So each item is a % of revenue from operations.
Answer: revenue from operations

quiz.q: In a common-size balance sheet, each item is expressed as a percentage of:
options: total assets (or total equity and liabilities)
quiz.explain: The balance sheet total is the base.
steps: In a common-size balance sheet, total assets (or total equity and liabilities) = 100.
So each item is a % of that total.
Answer: total assets (or total equity and liabilities)

quiz.q: Cost of materials consumed ₹6,00,000; revenue from operations ₹10,00,000. Common-size %:
steps: Common-size % = item ÷ revenue × 100.
Answer: 60%

quiz.q: Inventories ₹5,00,000; total assets ₹50,00,000. Common-size %:
steps: Common-size % = item ÷ total assets × 100.
Answer: 10%

quiz.q: Revenue ₹10,00,000 and total expenses ₹8,00,000. PBT as a common-size %:
steps: Answer: 20%

quiz.q: Trade payables ₹7,50,000; total equity and liabilities ₹50,00,000. Common-size %:
steps: Common-size % = item ÷ total equity and liabilities × 100.
Answer: 15%

quiz.q: Employee benefits were 10% of revenue last year and 14% this year. This indicates:
options: employee costs have risen faster than revenue
quiz.explain: A higher share of revenue means costs grew faster than revenue.
steps: Employee costs rose from 10% to 14% of revenue.
A bigger share means they grew faster than revenue.
Answer: employee costs have risen faster than revenue

quiz.q: The main advantage of common-size statements is that they:
options: remove the need for an audit
make comparison of firms of different sizes easy
quiz.explain: Percentages remove differences in scale.
steps: Percentages remove differences of scale.
So common-size statements make comparing firms of different sizes easy.
Answer: make comparison of firms of different sizes easy

teach.ask: Gappu wants to compare a big and a small company. Explain common-size statements.
teach.praise: Brilliant! Every item as a % of revenue or total assets – 100 is the base, and size no longer matters.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what is the base for a common-size balance sheet?

revise.summary: Common-size statements express each item as a percentage of a common base: revenue from operations for the Statement of Profit and Loss, and total assets for the balance sheet. They are vertical analysis and allow comparison across firms and years.
remember: Statement of P&L: % of revenue from operations
Balance sheet: % of total assets (or total equity and liabilities)
traps: Don't use the previous year's figure as base in a common-size statement
A rising % share means faster growth than the base, not an absolute fall
Balance sheet items are not expressed as % of revenue
